items.title: Europe’s Defence Coalitions Need Someone to Own the Outcome
items.summary: EU leaders are pushing capability coalitions. The next question is who is responsible when the capability does not materialise.

ai.sum: Analysis argues that EU defence capability coalitions need a clearly accountable owner when promised capabilities fail to materialise.

brief.summary: The author argues that EU capability coalitions are the right direction but face an accountability gap: European defence capacity is fragmented across national ministries, ports, railways, power grids, telecoms and private firms, and no institution owns the complete system. Rather than waiting for a single federal structure, he proposes starting with a few willing countries and a limited set of capabilities such as military mobility, logistics, air and missile defence, and surveillance. For each capability, a lead integrator (not a super-owner) would map the delivery chain, expose dependencies, monitor readiness and answer for whether the outcome can be produced. He suggests a 'Defence Capacity Statement' as a common discipline: required effect, usable capacity, critical dependencies, accountable owners and evidence. The Nordic and Baltic states are offered as a natural test case. The core message is outcome first, then visibility, control and accountability, with finance following capacity requirements.
brief.argument: Europe's fragmented defence capacity needs a designated lead integrator accountable for whether each agreed capability actually delivers its required outcome, rather than more coordination or a single common owner.
recommendations: Start with a small group of willing countries and a limited number of capabilities such as military mobility, logistics, air and missile defence, surveillance and energy resilience.
Designate a lead integrator for each agreed capability, responsible for the full delivery chain, unresolved dependencies, readiness and reporting on outcomes rather than ownership of assets.
Adopt a Defence Capacity Statement defining required effect, existing usable capacity, critical dependencies, accountable owners and evidence of delivery.
Map capabilities from the required outcome backwards, bringing civilian infrastructure owners such as ports, rail and grid operators into defence planning while keeping their ownership unchanged.

items.title: The Rising Threat of Great Power War and the Lessons of 1914
items.summary: History does not repeat, but sometimes it rhymes.

ai.sum: A CFR essay analyzes the rising threat of great power war by drawing lessons from 1914.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the post-Cold War optimism that great power war had been overcome has collapsed, as rivalry, nationalism and autocratic cohesion return. Drawing on a conversation with historian Odd Arne Westad, they compare today's dispersing, multipolar order to the years before 1914, when economic and political power shifted and nationalism rose. They stress that wars can begin without leaders choosing them, as escalation logic overrides prudent planning. Their central lesson is that policymakers must understand past mistakes and end small conflicts before they grow into something far larger. They also note that information moves faster and artificial intelligence increasingly places some decisions beyond human control, making the lesson more urgent. The piece is presented as an interview-based essay rather than a set of formal policy prescriptions.
brief.argument: Great power war is a rising risk because today's multipolar, nationalist world resembles the pre-1914 system, and leaders can be pushed into escalation they do not want, so small conflicts must be ended early.

ai.sum: Hudson Institute report challenges claims by I-MAK about drug patent evergreening in US pharmaceutical policy.

brief.summary: The authors, writing for Hudson Institute, argue that the Initiative for Medicines, Access, and Knowledge (I-MAK) drives congressional drug-patent policy with patent counts and exclusivity claims that do not survive scrutiny. They say I-MAK counts all patents and applications 'related to' a drug, including abandoned or irrelevant ones, and stacks their terms as 'evergreening'. The authors test I-MAK's claims on GLP-1 drugs and biologics, finding errors such as Lyrica and Rituxan, where generics or biosimilars entered years before I-MAK's claimed exclusivity ended. They conclude that the real evergreening is I-MAK's recurring brochures and its new Drug Patent Book, which keep feeding Washington with inaccurate claims, and that its numbers should not guide legislation.
brief.argument: I-MAK's patent counts and claimed exclusivity periods for drugs and biologics are methodologically unreliable and inaccurate, and they are being used to justify drug-patent legislation.
recommendations: Require I-MAK to disclose the specific patents and statistical methods behind its aggregate counts.

items.title: The G.I. and the Paperback: A World War II Love Story
items.summary: On June 5, 1944, as soldiers lined British shores, preparing for their perilous journey to the beaches of Normandy, Special Services units handed out comfort items, from packs of cigarettes to candy. But one item was more sought after than any other: books. Crouched on the crowded decks awaiting Eisenhower’s call to launch, the men clasped their standard-issue rifles and clutched their standard-issue paperbacks. They were armed with stories: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn,…

ai.sum: A historical account describes how paperback books were prized by US soldiers preparing for the Normandy landings in June 1944.

brief.summary: The author recounts how the Council on Books in Wartime, a group of civilian publishing figures, partnered with the US Army and Navy to produce Armed Services Editions: pocket-sized paperbacks distributed to servicemembers in World War II. The authors' lens is that the books met a niche need quickly and cheaply, with royalties set at one cent per copy. The piece argues that many servicemembers first read literature cover to cover through these books, which fed postwar growth in college attendance under the G.I. Bill and a paperback publishing boom. It concludes that today's defense planning, increasingly technical, might also benefit from simple, humane solutions delivered with civilian partners.
brief.argument: Simple, humane gifts delivered through civilian-military partnership can have lasting effects on servicemembers and society, as the Armed Services Editions did in World War II.
recommendations: Look for simple solutions to unmet servicemember needs that civilian partners can help deliver
Recognise that servicemembers' human needs for leisure and escape matter alongside technical capability

ai.sum: Jordanian airstrikes in southern Syria on 26 October killed 10 people, straining Jordan-Syria security cooperation to its lowest point since Assad's fall.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Jordan's airstrikes in southern Syria, which killed 10 people on 26 October, exposed the fragility of the Jordan-Syria rapprochement. Jordan says it coordinated the strikes and killed over 20 Islamic State members; Damascus says it had no advance notice, reports no IS casualties, and calls the strikes a sovereignty violation. The piece presents this as a test of Syria's 'zero problems' policy: diplomatic warming without effective security cooperation leaves cross-border threats likely to recur as diplomatic crises. Both governments have publicly chosen restraint and agreed a joint committee on the strikes, but the authors stress that the question of why Jordan bypassed Damascus remains unanswered and that the two states need to define mutual responsibilities and build a security partnership.
brief.argument: Without an effective security partnership, Jordan-Syria rapprochement remains fragile and cross-border threats risk becoming recurring diplomatic crises.
recommendations: Define mutual responsibilities on cross-border security between Damascus and Amman.
Build a security partnership capable of protecting people on both sides of the border.
Use the joint investigation committee to resolve disputes over intelligence and coordination.

ai.sum: Algeria deployed a military convoy into Niger for the first time since 1973 to secure oil-tanker convoys and protect pipelines.

brief.summary: The article examines Algeria's first military deployment into Niger since 1973, authorised by parliament after a late-2025 defence cooperation protocol with Niamey. The authors describe it as a move to secure Sonatrach's Kafra oilfield investments and the planned Trans-Saharan gas pipeline, and to safeguard Algeria's southern hinterland. They argue the venture faces serious risks: armed groups such as ISGS and Boko Haram cells exploiting the Salvador Triangle smuggling corridor, insurgent attacks on energy infrastructure, and cheap drones changing tactics. They also warn of friction with other outside powers in the Sahel, including Russia, Türkiye, Morocco and France, and conclude that Algeria's ability to protect its investments depends more on managing a multi-actor competition than on conventional military strength.
brief.argument: Algeria's Niger deployment is driven by energy-investment protection and border security, but it carries serious operational risks from non-state armed groups using drones and from competing foreign powers in the Sahel.
recommendations: Algiers should keep coordination channels open with Russia and Türkiye to avoid misunderstandings on the ground.
Algiers should protect energy infrastructure and supply lines while avoiding being drawn into Sahel proxy rivalries.
brief.turkey: Türkiye is named as a power with its own military engagement in the Sahel and with which Algiers has set up coordination channels, so Ankara's Sahel posture may need to account for Algerian-Turkish deconfliction.

items.title: Who Polices the Blockchain? The Binance Heist and the New Gatekeepers
items.summary: The institutions that have the authority to police international finance are no longer necessarily the institutions that possess the capabilities to do so.

ai.sum: RUSI analysis argues that institutions with policing authority over finance no longer necessarily have the capabilities to police crypto flows after the Binance case.

brief.summary: The author argues that the US$6.3 billion Binance heist, attributed in the piece to North Korean hackers, exposes a shift in who holds operational control over financial security. Criminals exploit digital finance, borders and speed, while governments keep legal authority but increasingly depend on private firms: stablecoin issuers that froze US$2.4 billion and blockchain analytics firms that tracked funds in near real time. The piece warns that this creates tension between legal authority and operational capability, and questions whether the FATF's government-centred standards are keeping pace. It concludes that freezing assets is not recovering them, and that the real test is how much illicit value is denied to its users.
brief.argument: Governments retain legal authority over financial security but now depend on private companies with superior operational capability, and the existing standard-setting model, led by the FATF, has not adapted to this shift.
recommendations: Set clear expectations on when private firms may unilaterally freeze assets, share information or intervene in transactions, with appropriate safeguards.
Connect private capabilities to public authorities so law enforcement and regulators can act at digital speed while preserving due process.
Radically re-examine the model on which the response to financial crime is built, since decades of standards have not kept up with the threat.

items.title: Is 2026 the New 1914?
items.summary: We Discuss: Mentioned on the Episode: Norman Angell, The Great Illusion, Simpkin, Marshall, Hamilton, Kent & Co. Odd Arne Westad, The Coming Storm: Power, Conflict, and Warnings from History, Allen Lane Odd Arne Westad, “Trump, Xi, and the Specter of 1914,” Foreign Affairs

ai.sum: A CFR podcast episode draws parallels between 2026 and 1914, citing Odd Arne Westad's warnings about US-China tensions.

brief.summary: The authors, in this CFR podcast with historian Odd Arne Westad, argue that today's multipolar, post-globalization world resembles the period before 1914 more than the Cold War or the 1930s. Westad holds that the economic gains of globalization have turned the countries that benefited most against it, as rising powers catch up, and that nationalism, populism and international terrorism have grown alongside. He stresses that World War I was not inevitable: leaders had many communication channels but lacked the willingness to play for time and did not understand each other's core strategic interests. Westad rejects the view that economic interdependence or nuclear weapons will reliably prevent great-power war, pointing to the 1914 precedent in which trade ties did not stop the war and to new weapons and proliferation that he considers unsettling. He also cautions that historical analogies carry real weight in policymaking and must be chosen and used with care.
brief.argument: Westad argues that the world of the 2020s resembles the pre-1914 era of globalization, rising powers and mutual misunderstanding, and that interdependence and nuclear deterrence are not reliable safeguards against great-power war.
recommendations: Use historical analogies with humility and accuracy, since policymakers reach for them under pressure.
Work to understand the core strategic interests of rival powers, not only to keep talking to them.
Do not assume economic interdependence will by itself deter war.

ai.sum: CFR podcast discusses the US economic fallout from the midterm elections and cost-of-living pressures voters prioritise.

brief.summary: The authors, host Rebecca Patterson and KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk, read the midterm results as voter frustration with inflation, health-care costs and stagnant wages, and see a mandate for Congress to focus on cost of living and affordability. They point to household debt strain, with about 20 percent of households behind on debt payments, and blame data center construction for pushing up electricity and water costs and wages in skilled trades. On the labour market they describe a 'low hire, low fire' economy with low turnover, and they note that real wages have lagged inflation for 13 straight months. They argue inflation is concentrated in food, energy and health care and that shocks have become endemic rather than episodic. Swonk argues the Fed should be more decisive, forecasting at least two rate hikes by early next year, and rejects the view that inflation near 3 percent is acceptable.
brief.argument: The authors argue that voters have signalled that cost-of-living pressures are their top priority and that the Fed should tighten decisively because inflation shocks have become persistent.
recommendations: Congress should focus on cost of living and affordability.
The Fed should raise rates, with at least two hikes by early next year.
Financial literacy should be expanded because it narrows the opportunity gap and strengthens the economy.

items.title: A $6 billion hack in a season of AI anxiety
items.summary: A $6.3 billion Binance hack and AI-assisted discoveries of software vulnerabilities made unsettling headlines. But not everything is as new or terrifying as it seems. The post A $6 billion hack in a season of AI anxiety appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: An Atlantic Council piece discusses a $6.3 billion Binance hack and AI-assisted discovery of software vulnerabilities.

brief.summary: The authors argue that recent headlines, a roughly $6 billion Binance theft and AI-assisted discovery of flaws in PHP and Node.js, should be separated into what is genuinely new and what is familiar. The Binance heist resembles earlier exchange breaches, attributed by the FBI to North Korea's TraderTraitor operation, with compromised credentials as the familiar weakness. What may be new is the speed at which stolen funds move, which reduces time to freeze assets. On AI-found bugs, they see a faster race between defenders and attackers, but note coordinated disclosure, early defensive AI testing by banks, and possible use of AI to repair aging code as grounds for guarded optimism. They conclude that existing laws, such as federal criminal statutes and negligence principles, can handle many questions, and that regulators should avoid sweeping new restrictions based on speculative AI risk.
brief.argument: Regulators should distinguish genuinely new AI-driven financial and cyber risks from familiar misconduct before adopting sweeping new restrictions.
recommendations: Distinguish genuinely new problems from familiar misconduct and concrete risks from conjecture before adding new restrictions
Apply existing criminal and negligence law where it suffices, reserving new rules for gaps
Extend defensive AI tools to critical infrastructure operators and open-source maintainers with limited resources
Use AI to proactively examine and repair aging internet code

items.title: Europe must weigh rising Ukraine costs against higher price of Russian victory
items.summary: If Russia succeeds in overrunning an underfunded and exhausted Ukraine, the consequences for Europe will be catastrophic and the price tag of stopping an emboldened Putin will dwarf the current cost of supporting Kyiv, writes Peter Dickinson. The post Europe must weigh rising Ukraine costs against higher price of Russian victory appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: An Atlantic Council commentary argues that the cost of stopping Russia in Ukraine is lower than the cost of a Russian victory for Europe.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Russia's escalated bombing of Ukraine's economic targets is deepening Kyiv's dependence on Western finance, with Ukraine reportedly needing about $80 billion more for 2027. They contend that the European debate over whether it can afford to keep funding Ukraine is the wrong frame, because a Russian victory would be far costlier. They point to occupation abuses, a possible flight of up to twenty million Ukrainians into the EU, a Russian-controlled Ukrainian army and defence industry on NATO's eastern flank, and the likely need to triple or quadruple European defence budgets. They also warn that Moscow is counting on European fatigue and on pro-Kremlin voices to block new aid, and that Europe must hold firm.
brief.argument: Europe should keep financing Ukraine because the cost of a Russian victory would far exceed the cost of sustaining Kyiv's war effort.
recommendations: Europe should find the additional funding Ukraine needs for 2027, with non-member states such as Japan, Norway, Switzerland, Canada and Britain asked to contribute more.
European governments should resist domestic populist pressure and the Kremlin-linked campaign against new aid.
Europe should rearm and expand its defence budgets to deter Russia regardless of the war's outcome.

items.title: A strong defense industry may be Ukraine’s best security guarantee
items.summary: Ukrainians have little faith in written guarantees and are well aware that nobody is going to fight Russia on their behalf. Instead, their most realistic security guarantee is a strong Ukrainian military backed by a powerful domestic defense industry, writes Leonid Baratz. The post A strong defense industry may be Ukraine’s best security guarantee appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: An Atlantic Council commentary argues that a strong domestic Ukrainian defense industry is Ukraine's most realistic security guarantee.

brief.summary: The authors argue that, with NATO membership unlikely and Coalition of the Willing guarantees limited by Russia's refusal of European troops, Ukraine's most realistic security guarantee is a strong domestic military backed by a powerful defence industry. They note Ukrainian output has grown sharply, with domestic drones causing most Russian losses, and that production capacity exceeds what the state can buy. They point to partners financing extra production as military aid, and to slow-moving export controls, high fees and administrative delays. They contend exports and joint ventures, especially in drones, would deepen integration into European security. They urge Kyiv to cut export fees and speed licensing, and European governments to buy Ukrainian systems for their own armies.
brief.argument: A strong, export-capable Ukrainian defence industry integrated into European security is a more realistic guarantee against future Russian invasion than written assurances or NATO membership.
recommendations: Kyiv should cut defence export fees and implement fast-track export licensing procedures.
European governments should finance Ukrainian production as military aid and also purchase Ukrainian systems for their own armies.
Expand joint ventures between Ukrainian and European defence companies, particularly in drones.

items.title: New Palestinian leaders will need more than an electoral mandate to govern
items.summary: The 2027 Palestinian elections will only give new leaders the authority to govern if they can control finances and security and rival factions agree to accept the results. The post New Palestinian leaders will need more than an electoral mandate to govern appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: An analysis argues that Palestinian elections planned for 2027 will only confer governing authority if new leaders control finances and security and rival factions accept results.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Palestinian diplomacy has expanded, through recognitions of Palestine and UN Security Council Resolution 2803, while Palestinian control over security and revenue has not. They contend the planned 2027 elections will only produce durable leadership if the winner controls a single budget and security command and unites Gaza's institutions with the West Bank's. They describe Israeli withholding of clearance revenues, settlement expansion such as the E1 tenders, and the Ramallah-Gaza split as obstacles, and say the Palestinian Authority will not reform itself without outside pressure. Their proposed lever is conditional Gulf and European funding, tied to verified reforms, with Washington pressing Israel to release revenues and keeping the Board of Peace temporary.
brief.argument: Palestinian elections will not yield a governing partner for negotiations unless the next leadership controls Palestinian finances and security and unifies Gaza with the West Bank before the transition.
recommendations: Consolidate rival Palestinian payrolls under one budget managed by one finance ministry, audited by the World Bank.
Place armed groups under a single command and require factions to accept the 2027 results and dismantle parallel institutions.
Release Gulf and European donor funds in tranches tied to verified reforms, and have Washington press Israel to release withheld clearance revenues.
Keep the Board of Peace strictly transitional, handing its powers on a fixed schedule to the government elected for both territories.

ai.sum: Michael Doran argues Trump should broker an Israeli unity government because political paralysis threatens Israel's ability to confront enemies.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Israel's October 27 election produced a deadlock: Netanyahu's bloc has 53 seats, Eisenkot's opposition 48, and Arab parties 19, short of the 61 needed. They contend the opposition failed because Eisenkot lacked executive experience and because the case blaming Netanyahu alone for October 7 rested on weak, Dahlan-linked sourcing, while the failure was systemic and included Eisenkot's own army doctrine. They judge the main minority-government route, relying on UTJ and Arab abstentions, as unstable and legitimacy-damaging, especially on war, Gaza, Syria and Iran decisions. They conclude that Israeli stability matters to Washington's wider strategy against Iran and China-led powers, and that a national unity government is the only workable option.
brief.argument: Israel's post-election deadlock can only be resolved by a national unity government, and Trump should broker it because Israeli governability serves US strategic interests.
recommendations: Trump should actively broker a national unity government between Netanyahu's and Eisenkot's blocs rather than merely observe.
Eisenkot should drop his veto on serving with Netanyahu and accept power-sharing.
Netanyahu should accept sharing power to keep his office.
Israeli leaders should agree a common security and budget programme, possibly with a temporary compromise on Haredi conscription.

items.title: The 2028 Presidential Race Is About to Begin
items.summary: Even as votes for the midterms elections are being counted, eyes are turning to the 2028 presidential election.

ai.sum: Attention in the US turns to the 2028 presidential race as midterm votes are still being counted.

brief.summary: The authors, writing for the Council on Foreign Relations, argue that the 2028 US presidential race effectively begins as the 2026 midterm votes are counted. They examine the Republican side, where Vice President JD Vance is the favourite but historically sitting vice presidents struggle to win the presidency, since distancing themselves from the incumbent risks alienating him and his base. On the Democratic side, Kamala Harris is the frontrunner, but the authors note recent open-race frontrunners have usually failed to win the nomination. They list many possible Democratic candidates and explain that the new Democratic primary calendar, opening in South Carolina, makes sequencing matter. The piece is largely historical and descriptive about US domestic electoral politics, with no foreign-policy argument.
brief.argument: Vance's incumbency gives him the lead for the Republican nomination, but history suggests sitting vice presidents rarely convert that position into the presidency, and Harris's frontrunner status in the Democratic race carries its own historical risks.

items.title: Foreign Policy and the 2026 Midterms: A CFR Guide
items.summary: A guide to CFR’s analysis, polling, videos, and podcasts on voter priorities, the global issues on the ballot, and the stakes after November 3.

ai.sum: CFR published a guide to its analysis and polling on foreign policy issues in the 2026 US midterm elections.

brief.summary: The authors examine how U.S. foreign policy is shaping the 2026 midterm campaign, arguing that the cost of living is voters' top concern but that the Iran war, tariffs, and related issues are feeding directly into gas prices, grocery bills and household budgets. Drawing on listening tours in Arizona and Wisconsin, polling reviews, podcasts and articles, they argue that foreign policy may carry unusual weight at the ballot box. Pieces cover voter attitudes toward the U.S. global role, the economic effects of tariffs (which they expect to be long-lasting regardless of the midterm outcome), Canada's resistance to trade pressure, Russia-linked disinformation amplified by AI chatbots, and possible U.S. escalation against Iran after November 3, alongside a warning about a debt-ceiling standoff in the lame-duck session.
brief.argument: Foreign policy issues such as the Iran war and tariffs are feeding directly into household costs, giving them outsized weight in the 2026 midterms.

items.title: Religion as statecraft: What a decade of research reveals about the geopolitics of religious soft power
items.summary: The post-Cold War assumption that international politics was converging toward a secular liberal framework in which religion would play at most a marginal role has not survived contact with the evidence. From China to Turkey to Saudi Arabia and Russia, states are integrating religion into their foreign policy in strategically significant ways. The post Religion as statecraft: What a decade of research reveals about the geopolitics of religious soft power appeared first on…

ai.sum: Atlantic Council analysis argues China, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Russia integrate religion into foreign policy as statecraft.

brief.summary: The authors argue that states across every major region now deliberately use religion as an instrument of foreign policy, and that this 'religious soft power' is a central, not peripheral, feature of great-power competition. Drawing on the eight-year Geopolitics of Religious Soft Power project, they contend that religious outreach serves domestic audiences as much as foreign ones, so the foreign and domestic logics are usually inseparable. They critique the Western 'moderate Islam' commodity, arguing the label often masks government efforts to delegitimise domestic opponents. They also stress that religious soft power is inherently competitive, with rival states such as Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Qatar, the UAE, Iran, Russia, China and India contesting the same religious audiences, and that the line between soft and sharp power is often deliberately blurred. The piece frames Western policymakers as having underweighted religion in their analyses.
brief.argument: Religion has become a deliberate, consequential instrument of statecraft whose domestic and foreign functions are usually inseparable and whose competitive dynamics Western policymakers have underweighted.
recommendations: Assess a partner government's religious outreach in light of its domestic political functions, not only its stated foreign policy framing.
Treat governments' claims to promote 'moderate Islam' with scepticism and ask moderate relative to whom.
Analyse religious soft power as a multi-actor competition rather than one state at a time.
brief.turkey: The piece treats the Diyanet's expansion and Turkey's religious outreach under the AKP as a case where foreign projection and domestic consolidation are intertwined, and as one contender in a competitive Sunni religious arena alongside the Gulf states.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the US Navy, despite being far larger than any rival, is planning for a twentieth-century fight: its fleet targets and composition largely mirror the Cold War force, and its shipbuilding plan is unsustainable in cost and manning. They contend that China's large and cheap missile arsenals, Russian pressure in Europe, and Iran's rapid reconstitution in the Gulf show that numbers of manned platforms no longer guarantee victory. Their alternative pairs a smaller, cheaper general-purpose fleet, with fewer carriers and surface combatants and more logistics and support ships, with tailored hedge forces for specific scenarios such as anti-submarine warfare, Persian Gulf mine clearance and defence of Taiwan. The hedge forces would draw on nearly 1,600 robotic and autonomous systems. The authors say this fleet would cost little above inflation and need about 50,000 fewer sailors than the Navy's plan, and they stress that the current window of rising funding and industrial acceleration should be used before it closes.
brief.argument: The US Navy should abandon its plan to rebuild a dominant manned fleet and instead build a sustainable, tailored force of manned ships plus large numbers of autonomous systems aimed at deterring and defeating specific likely threats.
recommendations: Shift the fleet mix toward submarines, logistics and support ships and away from large combatants relative to the current plan of record.
Replace the proposed Trump-class nuclear battleship with a guided missile cruiser.
Build a pool of about 1,600 robotic and autonomous systems that can be fitted with payloads and assigned to operational commanders.
Keep Navy budgets near the rate of inflation so the force remains robust against future defence spending cuts.

ai.sum: Analysis discusses quantum magnetometry in light of the rescue of an F-15E weapons systems officer during Operation Epic Fury.

brief.summary: The authors argue that quantum magnetometry is the most fieldable branch of quantum technology, despite the hype surrounding quantum computing and communication. They dismiss the reported "Ghost Murmur" heartbeat-detection story as physically implausible at long range, while affirming the underlying sensor physics. They describe how atomic vapor cells and nitrogen-vacancy diamond sensors detect faint magnetic fields, and how these support GPS-independent navigation, subterranean detection, submarine and mine hunting, and early counter-drone work. Their central concern is procurement and integration: they urge treating magnetometers as modular, platform-agnostic payloads, starting with high-payoff missions, and routing demand from theatre commanders to production through service acquisition executives and transition offices.
brief.argument: Quantum magnetometry is among the closest quantum technologies to operational use and should be fielded as modular payloads through faster procurement and integration, unlike the overhyped computing and communication branches.
recommendations: Treat quantum magnetometers as modular, retrofittable payloads rather than tying them to single platforms of record.
Have service acquisition executives, not individual program managers, make procurement decisions across platforms.
Start integration where the payoff is sharpest, fund in-context noise reduction, and build operator-friendly interfaces and multi-sensor fusion.

brief.argument: Voluntary pacing and self-disclosure by frontier AI labs cannot substitute for mandatory, externally auditable governance of agentic systems, especially in defence where oversight gaps are widest.
recommendations: Make reporting of serious agentic incidents mandatory to competent authorities, with guaranteed access for accredited independent evaluators.
Require legal and technical review of defence and cyber agentic systems across their lifecycle and acquisition, not only before deployment.
Build independent evaluation capacity outside the frontier labs so that expertise is not concentrated in the firms being assessed.

brief.argument: The EU-China auto deal is a good start, but containing China's export surge will require a much broader European trade and industrial response.
recommendations: Extend negotiated tariff-rate quotas and safeguards beyond autos to chemicals, machinery and other sectors where Chinese imports are surging.
Develop a broad, targeted tariff-based instrument, similar to a European Section 301, as a credible fallback if negotiations fail.
Adopt industrial policy tools, such as those in the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act, to require Chinese investors to localise more than final assembly in Europe.

items.title: Bibi and the Blockchain: When a Prime Minister Plans for Sanctions Evasion
items.summary: Benjamin Netanyahu’s interest in cryptocurrency reveals both the continuing power of financial sanctions and the current limits of technological attempts to circumvent them.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Benjamin Netanyahu's reported plan to build a crypto-based 'bypass economy' against possible sanctions misreads what sanctions do. Drawing on Russia's experience, they hold that crypto and stablecoins can move money for specific transactions and support circumvention networks, but cannot replicate the wider benefits of access to the international financial system, such as correspondent banking, trade finance, insurance and investment. They identify liquidity limits, stablecoin risk and the need for counterparties to rewire payments as obstacles at national scale. They also stress that financial sovereignty depends on other actors' willingness to trust and accept the system, and that circumvention is not substitution. The piece concludes that governments seeking protection from isolation should focus on preventing sanctions rather than building alternative payment rails.
brief.argument: Crypto can move money for specific transactions but cannot substitute for the broader access to the international financial system that a sanctioned economy needs.
recommendations: Focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy rather than building alternative payment systems.
Recognise that crypto offers payment transfer but not guaranteed counterparties, credit, insurance or investment.
Treat sanctions evasion as requiring a range of tools rather than a single crypto solution.

brief.argument: China's new mobilisation law, set within a decade-long securitisation of the state, gives Beijing a legal basis to sustain a long war and to mobilise resources in disputes such as Taiwan.
